(1.26) If one asks: "How is it that one who is devoid of ethical discipline does not attain prosperity? It is because, through the force of the exhaustion of the karma that projected the previous existence, one falls into an evil rebirth. Furthermore, even if one is born among humans, one is dull-witted and poor. Therefore, it

When he is independent and does not direct his own thoughts toward the state of meditative equipoise, who indeed will raise him up later when he has fallen into the abyss of a cave and attained a state of dependence on others? (Madhyamakakārikā 2.5)

Thus it has been said: if, at that time, he remains in a favorable region like a hero released from bondage, acting according to his own will and not having entered into subjection to others, and while dwelling in the worlds of gods and humans does not reflect upon himself—
then who will later raise him up when he has fallen into an evil rebirth, like a bound hero abandoned in a most formidable cave?

For this very reason, there will certainly be a miserable rebirth (*durgati*) as a result of that affliction. Furthermore, it is said that even when one is reborn among humans, two kinds of maturation (*paripāka*) are established;
because such a person of immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*) is the locus for an accumulation of exceedingly great faults.
Then the Jina, having expounded the discourse on generosity, spoke the discourse concerning ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Therefore, the Jina—who has conquered all unwholesome qualities—immediately after the discourse on generosity, delivered the discourse on ethical discipline so that the virtues of generosity and the rest would not be lost.
Indeed, when virtue has increased upon the ground of ethical discipline, the enjoyment of its fruit will be continuous. (Madhyamakakārikā 2.6)
Because it is the locus of all virtuous qualities, ethical discipline (*śīla*) itself is the ground.

In that regard, the progressive increase of all virtues such as generosity and so forth constitutes a succession of cause and effect; by gradually augmenting the equipment of results (*phala-sambhāra*) in an uninterrupted manner, it enables one to enjoy them for a long time, whereas otherwise it does not.
Therefore, in this manner:

"For the Son of the Conqueror, who abides in the nature of his own enlightenment as distinct from that of ordinary persons and Śrāvakas, there is no cause for worldly prosperity other than ethical discipline (śīla), nor is there any other cause for the supreme good. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 2.7)

For example: "Furthermore, these ten unwholesome paths of action, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed to an excessive degree, are the cause for rebirth in hell; to a middling degree, they are the cause for rebirth as an animal; and to a mild degree, they are the cause for the world of Yama.
Among them, the taking of life leads one to hell, leads one to the animal realm," and so forth.
It leads one to the world of Yama;
or, if one is reborn among humans, it brings about two results: a short lifespan and much illness.

Taking what is not given... [and so forth]... results in meager wealth and shared wealth. Sexual misconduct... results in having an undisciplined retinue and having a spouse with rivals. False speech... results in being frequently slandered and being deceived by others.
Slander leads to having a divided retinue and having a lowly retinue.
Harsh speech leads to hearing what is unpleasant and uttering words of strife.
Frivolous chatter leads to one's words being disregarded and one’s eloquence being uncertain.
Covetousness leads to lack of contentment and great desire;
ill-will leads to wishing harm and the oppression of others;
and wrong view leads to hell.
It leads one to the animal realm, it leads one to the world of Yama;
yet, if one is reborn among humans, [it leads one there].
He brings about two types of maturation: he falls into wrong views and becomes deceitful and fraudulent.
Thus, indeed, these ten unwholesome paths of action lead to the origination of a great and immeasurable mass of suffering.
Furthermore, by reason of undertaking the wholesome paths of action, rebirths are known to exist, beginning from birth among gods, humans, and so forth, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

Beyond that, those same ten paths of wholesome action, when cultivated through the mode of wisdom, lead to the Śrāvaka vehicle by virtue of a limited mind, a mind terrified of the three realms, an absence of great compassion, and by following what is heard from others and following the sound.
Beyond even that, when further purified by not being led by others, by being conducive to self-becoming, and by attaining self-enlightenment—
By not seeking from others, by being devoid of great compassion and skillful means, and by awakening to this profound conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā*),
it leads to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Beyond that, when further purified, it becomes vast through its immeasurability, endowed with great compassion, and embraced by skillful means.
"Because they are bound by great vows, because they do not abandon any sentient being, and because they have the vast cognition of a Buddha as their objective support,

they lead to the purification of the bodhisattva stages, the purification of the perfections, and the expansion of conduct. Having thus spoken at length, it follows that in this manner, beyond those ten paths of wholesome action, there exists for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, according to their respective capacities, [the cause] of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*).
It has been taught that there is no other means for attaining *niḥśreyasa*—which is characterized by liberation and has the nature of the absence of pleasure and pain—than this.
As for that Bodhisattva who has generated the second thought of awakening: just as the ocean, even with a corpse and even with that which is inauspicious, remains auspicious; so too is he.
For thus it is said: "A great being who is devoted to ethical discipline does not dwell together with those of corrupt discipline. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 2.8)
"Inauspicious" (*amaṅgala*) is a synonym for the unwholesome (*akuśala*). As it was stated in the explanation of the divisions of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*):
"From what, what, and where is that which is called ethical discipline abandoned when the threefold [classification] is grasped?"
They call that the mundane perfection;
when that morality is dependent upon the three, it is designated as a mundane perfection.
That which is supramundane is empty of the three [poisons], such as passion. (Madhyamakakārikā 2.9)
If that very morality should be devoid of the three aforementioned objects of focus, it is called the supramundane perfection.
By way of restating the qualities of the stages as described, he speaks of the complete perfection of the state of the perfection of morality:
"Though stainless like the moon arisen from the sons of the Victors, this Vimalā is the glory of existence, yet free from becoming and non-becoming."
Like the moonlight of the autumn season, it dispels the mental anguish of the world.
"Vimalā" (The Stainless) is the name of the second bodhisattva stage, given according to its literal meaning because it is stainless due to the ten paths of wholesome action.

Just as the stainless light of the autumn moon dispels the heat of the people, so too does this stainless [stage], when the moon of the Conqueror’s Son has arisen, turn back the mental anguish produced by immoral conduct.
Because it is not included within saṃsāra, it is not "existence" (bhava), but rather the "glory of existence" (bhavaśrī).
Because it follows upon all perfections of virtue and because it is the cause for the perfection of sovereignty over the four continents;
thus ends the second production of the thought [of awakening] in the *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya*.
3. The Third Arising of the Thought of Enlightenment:
Now, with reference to the third arising of the thought of enlightenment, it is said:
Because of the emergence of the radiance of the fire that burns the fuel of all objects of knowledge without exception, this is the third stage.
*Prabhākarī*... *Prabhākarī* is the name of the third bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, if one asks why this is called *Prabhākarī*, it is because the name is indeed literal (*anvartha*).
At that time, because the light consisting of tranquility arises from the fire of gnosis (*jñāna*) which burns the fuel of all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), this stage is called *Prabhākarī*.
With the arising of the third thought-moment... that son of the Sugata then shines like the copper-colored sun. *Madhyamakakārikā* 3.1.
Just as [the sun] appears like copper before its state of rising, so too does knowledge appear within the Bodhisattva.
For the sake of teaching the excellence of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) of that Bodhisattva who has attained such an appearance of knowledge, it is said:
"If someone were to cut from his body, along with the bone and flesh, him who is a vessel for non-anger."
Even as his body is being cut piece by piece, his patience toward the executioner is exceedingly great.

Because a bodhisattva acts for the sake of protecting the minds of others and possesses such knowledge, there is no witness who can observe his nature, body, speech, and mind in such a way that they would become a basis for the hatred of others, be useless across the three times, or become a source of doubt. This is so unless there is some specific qualification regarding one who is not a fit vessel for anger.

Even if such a being were to cut away the flesh and bone from that bodhisattva’s body, pausing again and again for a long time, the bodhisattva would not only feel no mental resentment toward such a cutter; rather, by reflecting on the specific sufferings of hell and so forth resulting from the conditions of those unwholesome deeds, an exceptionally distinguished patience arises within the bodhisattva. Moreover—

Since that Bodhisattva, seeing with the vision of selflessness, perceives all phenomena as being like reflections, how, by what means, and what could there be to be cut off? Or rather, at what time does he attain patience? (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.3)
Relying on the specific sufferings of hell and other realms conditioned by those unwholesome karmas, he is not only exceptionally patient; moreover,
because he perceives all phenomena as being like reflections and has turned away from the notions of "self" and "mine," he is for that reason even more patient.
The word "also" (*api*), however, is for the purpose of including the cause of patience.

This patience is not only a quality appropriate to a bodhisattva, but because it serves as the cause for protecting all other virtues as well, the turning away from anger—just like patience itself—is also appropriately explained: "If one becomes angry with a wrongdoer, what would be achieved here by that anger? It would merely be the anger that has been provoked which is turned back."
Therefore, anger toward this is indeed pointless; it is also quite contrary [to one's interest] in the world beyond. (Madhyamakakārikā 3.4)

Now, this is the occasion for giving vent to anger; if one becomes angry with an external wrongdoer at that time, it is entirely useless because the harm already committed cannot be undone, as the deed has already been performed.
Anger toward this person is not only useless in the present, but it is also detrimental to the next world; for when anger arises, it projects an undesirable ripening of results.

One who, experiencing the specific fruit of the karma of misconduct, imagines out of delusion that "I am being oppressed by another," gives rise to anger toward the wrongdoer and desires to overcome that oppression through retaliation— against such a person,
for the sake of turning them away [from this], he says: "But as for one who wishes to regard the fruit of previously committed unwholesome karma as something already destroyed."
Since suffering arises precisely from anger directed at others, how could that [anger] ever be brought about as the seed of that [suffering]? (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.5)

The most grievous suffering of harm inflicted upon his body by an enemy through the falling of weapons is the final fruit of that being’s own previously committed karma of taking life; it is the terrible ripening fruit experienced in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, as well as the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) which serves as the cause for producing all remaining unpleasant results of the residual afflictions.
How, then, can it be said that [anger] is subject to transformation?

Because, like the final dose of medicine which serves as the cause for curing a disease within its own duration, anger—though resulting in past disagreeable fruits through malice and injury to others—is a cause for the possibility of even more distinguished fruits of harm;

therefore, just as a physician’s performance of a sharp surgical procedure, which is the cause for treating a disease, is rightly met with extreme forbearance despite being a cause for the arising of suffering from its fruit, so too should this be treated.

However, intolerance is not only the cause for the rejection and the ripening of what is unpleasant; it is also the cause for the destruction of the accumulation of merit gathered over a long period. To teach this, it is said: "The merit accumulated over a hundred eons through generosity and ethical discipline may perish in an instant through anger toward the Sons of the Conquerors. Therefore, there is indeed no evil other than anger. (Madhyamakakārikā 3.6)

If that great-souled bodhisattva, due to entering under the influence of habitual afflictions, imputes excessive— whether real or unreal— faults to another person, whether distinguished or undistinguished, then by the mere arising of a single moment of anger, even for that brief duration, the entire accumulation of merit gathered over a hundred eons through the practice of the previously mentioned perfections of generosity and ethical discipline is destroyed.
If even an ordinary person can generate [the thought of awakening] toward Bodhisattvas, what more need be said when it is generated by one who is not a Bodhisattva?
Therefore, just as the volume of water in the great ocean cannot be determined by counting grains of sand, so too the limit of maturation therein cannot be determined.
Consequently, this being the case, there is no evil greater than intolerance (*akṣānti*), which projects unpleasant fruits and causes the exhaustion of merit.
“Mañjuśrī, ‘anger, anger’ is so called because it causes the exhaustion of the merit accumulated over a hundred eons; therefore, it is designated as ‘anger.
Furthermore, those who are intolerant and unable to retaliate against the harm done by others destroy only themselves.”
They are capable and merciless, bringing ruin to both themselves and others;
but this one, from birth itself,
was raised by evil people, possessed false views, and was devoid of the discrimination that distinguishes right from wrong conduct.
At a later time, having abandoned the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), one who is prone to anger quickly goes to an evil rebirth.
If these are the faults of impatience (*akṣānti*), then what indeed are the virtues of its opposite, patience (*kṣānti*)?
For virtues are said to be contradictory when there is no absence of anger. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.7)
There is loveliness of appearance, the conduct of a virtuous person, and proficiency in discerning right from wrong;
thereafter, birth as a god or human follows, for through the absence of anger, evil comes to an end. (Madhyamakakārikā 3.8)
Those faults of impatience (*akṣānti*) which have been described should be understood as the virtues of patience (*kṣānti*), being their opposites. That is to say:

having clearly perceived the faults and virtues of anger and patience respectively, both the ordinary person and the Son of the Victor should immediately cast aside anger and always rely upon patience, which is praised by the noble ones. (Madhyamakakārikā 3.9)
But anger and patience are [defined] by anger and patience themselves;
likewise, faults and virtues are [defined] by faults and virtues.
This is the application of the terms "faults and virtues" to anger and patience.
Since the fault of anger has been explained as stated above,
one should understand the virtue of patience through its opposite, abandon impatience, and at all times rely upon patience alone.
Now, for the purpose of teaching the divisions of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā):
If even the dedication for the sake of the enlightenment of a perfectly awakened one is based on the three [spheres], it is indeed mundane.
Even in the case of dedication toward Buddhahood, what is the receptivity,
and by whom is there receptivity?

In which living beings does this patience exist? It exists when these three bases are present; this perfection of patience is thus worldly. Indeed, that same patience, when it is non-reliant, is taught by the Buddhas as the supramundane perfection.

On that stage, just as the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience becomes purified, so too—on this stage, the Son of the Victor, having destroyed passion and enmity, possesses the superknowledges and meditative concentrations;
he is capable of utterly destroying the worldly passions of desire. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.11)

Regarding the term "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*), the word *dhyāna* is used as an inclusive designation (*upalakṣaṇa*), which includes the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) as well.
As it was stated in the Third Bodhisattva Stage (*Bodhisattvabhūmi*): "Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage called the Radiant (*Prabhākarī*)," and so forth.

For the sake of practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, the bodhisattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences with his body that bliss of which the Noble Ones say, "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in bliss. Thus, having attained the third dhyāna, free from joy, he dwells therein.

“With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. These are the four dhyānas.

The four formless attainments are as follows: "By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] 'space is infinite,' one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, [thinking] 'consciousness is infinite,' one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness."
“By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, [thinking] ‘there is nothing at all,’ he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, [thinking] ‘neither perception nor non-perception,’ he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.
These are the four formless attainments.

The four immeasurables are as follows: "With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, unobstructed, and harmless—he dwells having suffused and attained the entire world, extending everywhere throughout the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), reaching to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*).
Likewise with a mind accompanied by compassion..."
He dwells with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy;
he dwells with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
As for the five supernormal knowledges:
For example: "He experiences various kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhividhi*):
he causes even the earth to tremble;
having been one, he becomes many."
Having become many, he becomes one again;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance as well.
He passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains, just as if through space.
He travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
he performs the act of diving and surfacing in the earth as if in water;
and he walks upon the water without sinking, just as on the earth.
He emits smoke and blazes up,
just like a great mass of fire;
he also releases great torrents of water from his own body, just like a great cloud.
"By means of those streams of water, this trichiliocosm—blazing, aflame, and fiercely burning with fire, having become a single mass of flame—is extinguished.

He even touches and strokes with his hand these two, the sun and moon, who possess such great supernatural power (maharddhika) and such great majesty (mahānubhāva), and he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
These are the supernormal powers of psychic transformation (ṛddhyabhijñā).
“With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds— the divine and the human, the subtle and the gross;
he hears sounds whether they are far or near, even down to those of gadflies, mosquitoes, insects, and flies.”
[This is the divine supernormal power of the ear.
“He understands, as it truly is, the mind of other beings and other persons with his own mind.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind possessed of lust as a mind possessed of lust.”
He understands a dispassionate mind as "dispassionate mind"; he understands a mind with hatred as "with hatred," and a mind with delusion as "with delusion."
free from delusion,
with afflictions, and without afflictions;
limited, vast,
and immeasurable.
immeasurable, contracted, [and expanded].
concentrated,
unconcentrated,
and liberated;
The Unreleased,
with limb, and without limb.
He understands as it really is a gross mind as "a gross mind," and he understands as it really is a non-gross mind as "a non-gross mind.
Thus, with his own mind, he understands as it really is the minds of other beings and other persons.
[Thus is this supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others. “He recollects his manifold past abodes; he recollects even a single birth.”
He recollects two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred thousand births;
even many hundreds of births,
many thousands of births, and many hundreds of thousands of births.
He recollects even a *saṃvarta*-kalpa (aeon of dissolution), even a *vivarta*-kalpa (aeon of evolution), and even many aeons of both dissolution and evolution; he recollects even a hundred aeons,
a thousand aeons, a hundred thousand aeons, ten million aeons, and even a billion aeons.

He recollects even a thousand *koṭīs* of eons, even a hundred thousand *koṭīs* of eons, and even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons: "In that time, I was named such-and-such; I belonged to such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a caste, had such-and-such food, such-and-such a lifespan, and remained for such-and-such a duration; I experienced such-and-such pleasure and pain. Having passed away from there, I was reborn here."
"Having passed away from there, I was reborn here"—
thus he recollects his manifold former abodes with their modes, details, and causes.
[This is the supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes.]”
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—fair and ugly, in happy states and miserable states, exalted and lowly;

he understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma: "These worthy beings, possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, possessed of misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones..."

Those with wrong views, due to the cause of undertaking actions based on wrong views, and with that as their cause and condition, are reborn after the breaking up of the body, after death, in states of woe, in evil destinies, in perdition, and in the hells.
But these beings, sirs, are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; they do not revile the noble ones.

He understands that "due to the cause of undertaking actions with right view, and with that as their cause and condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings— both those passing away and those being reborn— with their forms, their locations, and their characteristics.
He understands beings as they truly are according to the karma they have undergone;
he enters into and emerges from these meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
And he is not reborn under their power; rather, wherever he perceives the fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment, there he is reborn intentionally by the power of his vow.
Why is that?
Because the mental continuum of that bodhisattva has been brought forth through skill in means.”

For this very reason, although meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arise for the Bodhisattva on this stage, how is there the constant destruction of worldly passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*)?
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned;
thus, there is also the destruction of that delusion (*moha*). How so?
This also is as stated in the Sūtra: “He contemplates all phenomena by way of their dependent origination, [seeing] their non-transmigration and their indestructibility.”
To a still greater degree, all his fetters of sensual desire become attenuated;
all his fetters of form, all his fetters of existence, and all his fetters of ignorance become attenuated;
and the fetters consisting of views have already been abandoned.
For that Bodhisattva established in this Prabhākari Bodhisattva-bhūmi, for many eons,
even up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— [as the text continues]— false passion (*mithyārāga*) comes to abandonment without further accumulation,
and false hatred (*mithyādoṣa*) comes to abandonment without further accumulation.
"It is said that false delusion, which does not accumulate, goes toward abandonment.
Therefore, for such a person, lust, hatred, and delusion become utterly exhausted.
For how will they be able to always overcome worldly sensual desire? As it has been said: "O sons of the Conqueror, this is the third bodhisattva stage of the Bodhisattva, named *Prabhākarī*.

Established in this stage, the Bodhisattva for the most part becomes Indra, the king of the gods and lord of the Thirty-three, a capable master, skilled in applying the means for turning beings away from sensual desire, and able to lift beings out of the mire of sense-pleasures. Thus it was stated.
Therefore, that Son of the Conqueror will become capable of destroying worldly desire for sensual pleasures.

Thus, for this Bodhisattva on the third Bodhisattva stage, there will be the purification of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the immeasurable meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the attainments (*samāpatti*), and the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), as well as the certain attainment of the complete exhaustion of passion and the other [afflictions]. Having said this, [the text now addresses] up to the limit of the perfection of patience.
In order to elucidate the distinction of the basis of the three perfections, the nature of the accumulations, and the establishment of the perfection of the fruit, it is said:
"These three dharmas consisting of giving and so forth were taught by the Sugatas especially for householders;
when these very same [dharmas] are accumulated as merit, they are the cause of the body whose nature is the form of a Perfectly Awakened One. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.12)

Although only bodhisattvas possess the aforementioned foundations such as generosity and so forth, it was stated in that way after considering the possibility of these two [categories] existing therein through the distinction between householders and renunciants.
Among them, for householders, the three dharmas beginning with generosity are generally easy to accomplish.
Among the wandering mendicants as well, there is energy,
meditative concentration, and likewise wisdom;
yet there is no mutual lack of confidence between them.
However, there are two accumulations that serve as the causes for Buddhahood:
namely, the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of knowledge.
Among these, the accumulation of merit consists of those three perfections.
The equipment of knowledge consists of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*),
while vigor (*vīrya*) is established as the cause for both.

In that regard, the equipment of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*) is the cause for the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) of the Blessed Fully Enlightened Ones— a body consisting of all forms, marvelous, inconceivable, and characterized by a hundred marks of merit.
The cause of the body of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāvakāya*), which is characterized by non-arising, is the equipment of gnosis (*jñānasambhāra*).
Having now described its own greatness through the majesty of its basis (*āśraya*) and so forth, the state of the third bodhisattva stage is explained:
"In this Radiant stage (*prabhākarī*), the sun-like son of the Conqueror first destroys his own darkness."
The sun that is the Son of the Sugata, abiding on this Prabhākarī (Luminous) stage, strives to dispel the darkness of ignorance inherent within itself; having destroyed that ignorance—

which acts as an obstacle to its own arising— at the very moment it is born, it strives to dispel the darkness that obstructs the emergence of the third stage for others through its instruction on those methods.
That Bodhisattva does not feel anger toward this earth, even though it has become harsh. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 3.13)

However, by destroying the darkness of faults that act as obstacles, he does not become angry even when descending with extreme sharpness like the sun toward people possessed of faults; this is due to his exceptionally distinguished practice of patience, his compassion, and the gentleness of his mental continuum. This concludes the third generation of the mind in the *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya*.
4. The Fourth Arousing of the Mind:

Now, by way of teaching the excellence of the perfection of vigor over the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, the fourth arousal of the mind is explained with reference to it:
"Having followed after all virtues through vigor, it is the cause of the two accumulations of wisdom and merit."
Since from that very point vigor becomes truly radiant, that is indeed the fourth stage, the Radiant (arciṣmatī).
However, in a state consisting of a lack of enthusiasm for wholesome actions, since there is no engagement in giving and so forth in any way, the arising of all virtues is impossible.

But for one who is eager to accumulate the previously mentioned collection of virtues, because the increase of what has been attained and the attainment of what has not yet been attained are possible, diligence alone is the cause of any virtue whatsoever.
As for the cause of the two accumulations, it has already been explained previously.
That energy which blazes forth on a certain stage by way of the complete purification of its own qualities is the fourth bodhisattva stage, and it shall be called *Arciṣmatī* (The Radiant).
Furthermore, for what reason is it designated as *Arciṣmatī*? It is for the purpose of teaching the cause of its entry [into that name]:
"Because of the manifestation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*sambodhipakṣa*), a radiance is born in the Son of the Sugata."

It has been stated that it shines more intensely than the Tāmraprabhā [ground]. Thus, on this ground, through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), a radiance arises in the Bodhisattva that is superior to the previously described Tāmraprabhā.
Therefore, because it is produced by the light of the fire of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), this Bodhisattva ground is called Arciṣmatī (The Radiant).
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are as follows: the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa),
and the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
The five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path have been explained.
In that regard, there are the four foundations of mindfulness: "O Sons of the Conqueror,

a bodhisattva established on this Radiant Bodhisattva Stage dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world."
He dwells contemplating the body in the external body—
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world— both internally and externally with respect to the body.

In the same way, he dwells contemplating feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally; likewise, he dwells contemplating the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally; and he dwells contemplating phenomena in relation to internal phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
"...contemplating phenomena in external phenomena... thus [he contemplates] internally and externally in regard to phenomena," as detailed in the extensive explanation.
The four right efforts are as follows: "He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, and applies his mind for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states..."
He exerts himself and applies himself correctly for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen [as previously described].
[As before: He generates the desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
and for the stability, non-confusion, expansion, increase, cultivation, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
He exerts himself as before:

"The four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda): he cultivates the base of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment, which is determined by seclusion, determined by dispassion, determined by cessation, and results in relinquishment; likewise for energy..."

“He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of concentration and abandonment; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of mind; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of investigation,” and so forth, as previously described.

The five faculties are as follows: “He cultivates the faculty of faith... [as before] ...determined by seclusion... the faculty of energy... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom... He...
“He cultivates that which is determined by dispassion,” and so forth.
As for the five powers, they are those very same [faculties] when undefeated by their opposing factors, as previously described.
The seven factors of enlightenment are as follows: (he) ...
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, and so forth;

he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment that is energy, the factor of enlightenment that is joy, the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity— and so forth, as previously described.

The Noble Eightfold Path is as follows: “He cultivates right view— [resolved upon dispassion, resolved upon cessation, ripened in relinquishment]— right intention [also as before]— right speech……right action……right livelihood……right effort……right mindfulness……right concentration” [he cultivates, etc., as before].
On this stage, not only does the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening arise, but also: "The attachment to the view of self is utterly destroyed. (Madhyamaka-kārikā 4.2)

On this stage, there also occurs for him the destruction of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Thus it is said: "O Sons of the Victor, for a Bodhisattva established on this *Arciṣmatī* Bodhisattva-stage, those bases of habitation—which are preceded by the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which arise from the attachment to a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, a human, a *pudgala*, and to the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; which have been wiped away and submerged, pondered and reflected upon, cherished, claimed as 'mine,' treasured, and established as dwellings—[are all abandoned]."
"All those [obscurations] have become vanished. Thus it was said.
This concludes the fourth production of the thought of awakening, named "The Radiant," in the *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya*.
5. The fifth production of the thought of awakening.
Now begins the section on the fifth production of the thought of enlightenment:
that great being who has reached the stage of "Difficult to Conquer" (durjayā-bhūmi) is indeed incapable of being defeated even by all the Māras.

A Bodhisattva established in the fifth Bodhisattva stage cannot be conquered even by the Devaputra-Māras residing in all the world-systems; what need then be said of others, such as the servants of Māra and the like?

For this very reason, the name of this stage is "Very Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā). However, the Bodhisattva is preeminent in meditative concentration (dhyāna) and, possessing excellent intelligence, is exceedingly skillful in realizing the subtle nature of reality. (Madhyamakakārikā 5.1)
It should be understood that among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) alone is preeminent.
"Sumati" refers to the Noble Ones (*ārya*); the truths of those who possess excellent wisdom are the "truths of Sumati," which is to say, the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is one's own form (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, an intrinsic nature that is realized through subtle knowledge is a "subtle intrinsic nature";
one who possesses excellent intelligence becomes exceedingly skillful in knowing the subtle form of the truths.
The four noble truths, however, are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Yet, the Blessed One has taught that there are only two truths, namely: conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
As it is said in the *Pitāputrasamāgama-sūtra*:
These two truths were taught by the Knower of the World himself, without having heard them from others:
the conventional and likewise the ultimate; no third truth is established.
Thus it has been said.
Also, in the Madhyamakaśāstra: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths."
The truth of worldly convention and the truth from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus it has been said.

If it is asked, "In that case, do other four noble truths exist apart from non-duality?"—it is explained: although this is so, nevertheless, the four noble truths are taught here for the purpose of showing the distinct causal and fruitional relationships between that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted.
In that context, the side to be abandoned consists of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
its fruit being the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*),
and its cause being the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
The category of what is to be adopted, however, is purification; its fruit is the truth of cessation,
and the cause for attaining that is the truth of the path.
Among these, the truths of suffering, origin, and the path are included within conventional truth;
the truth of cessation is the very nature of ultimate truth.
Furthermore, whatever other truths there may be, it should be determined that they too are included within these two truths according to their respective application.
If it is asked, "Is there another truth beyond the four truths? it has been explained.
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the fifth stage: "One understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of suffering';
one understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering'..."
He understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering";
he understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
He becomes skilled in conventional truth.
He becomes skilled in the ultimate truth;
he becomes skilled in the truth of characteristics; and he becomes skilled in the truth of distinctions.
He becomes skilled in the truth of transcendence,
skilled in the truth of entities,
and skilled in the truth of origination.
He becomes skilled in the truths of cessation and non-arising;
he becomes skilled in the truths for entering the knowledge of the path;
and through the accomplishment of the continuous progression through all the stages of a bodhisattva, he becomes skilled in the truth of the origination of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
By satisfying the intentions of other beings as they are, he understands conventional truth;
by the convergence into a single principle, he understands ultimate truth;
and by the realization of specific and general characteristics, he understands the truth of characteristics.
Through the awakening to the establishment of the classification of phenomena (*dharma*), one understands the truth of classification;
through the awakening to the establishment of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), one understands the truth of investigation;
and because it is encountered as an affliction to the body of the mind, it is the truth of the factual basis (*vastu*).
The truth of origination is so called because it binds one to the connection of the realms of existence;

the truth of cessation is so called because it brings about the absolute pacification of all fevers and burning pains, as well as the non-arising of exhaustion; [and the truth of non-dual non-arising.]
“Because of the realization of non-duality, one enters the truth of the knowledge of the path;

through the complete awakening to all aspects and the accomplishment of the sequential progression through all the bodhisattva stages, one thoroughly understands the truth of the arising of the Tathāgata’s gnosis,” so it was said.
Thus ends the fifth generation of the mind of awakening, named "Very Difficult to Conquer," in the commentary on the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.
